svg.aria-label: Diagram: Lambda is responsible for curating and publishing security updates for all supported managed runtimes and container images, but responsibility for updating existing Event Functions to use the latest runtime version varies depending on the runtime update mode. There are three modes. In Auto mode Lambda applies runtime updates to all functions configured to use it, and the customer's responsibility is to roll back in the rare event of an incompatibility. In Function update mode Lambda applies runtime updates when you update your function, and the documentation states that if you don't update your function then Lambda doesn't update the runtime, so a function nobody deploys stops being patched; AWS recommends switching such functions to Auto. In Manual mode you are responsible for updating to the latest version, and the mode is documented for use only as a temporary rollback in the rare event of a compatibility issue. Two further deployment shapes have their own splits: with container images Lambda publishes updated base images and you are responsible for rebuilding from the latest base image and redeploying, and with a customer-managed runtime the runtime publisher rather than Lambda publishes versions with the latest patches and updates runtime aliases, while Lambda applies whatever version the alias points to according to the function's update mode. There is no deadline: Lambda does not impose a time limit on how long you can use a particular runtime version, but functions using an earlier version for an extended period might eventually experience degraded performance or issues such as a certificate expiry which can cause them to stop working properly, so the failure arrives as a cliff rather than a slope with no banner, blocked deployment or API error beforehand. Published function versions are immutable snapshots of code and configuration, and the runtime underneath them follows the mode: in Auto mode Lambda updates the runtime version of published function versions during phase two of a rollout, while in Function update mode it does not, which makes those published versions a static snapshot of code, configuration and runtime that is excellent for reproducible rollback and is simultaneously a frozen runtime unless you publish regularly. If the dollar-LATEST version uses Manual mode you cannot change the CPU architecture or runtime version. Finally the posture is enforceable rather than requested: denying access to the PutRuntimeManagementConfig API operation causes all functions to default to Auto mode, this can be applied organisation-wide with a service control policy, and for customer-managed runtimes denying lambda:AssociateRuntimeVersion prevents pinning to specific runtime versions.
svg.title: Lambda publishes the patch; the update mode decides whether it reaches you
svg.text: Publishing and applying are different jobs. AWS only does the first unconditionally.
“Responsibility for updating existing Event Functions to use the latest runtime version varies depending
on which runtime update mode you use.”
Three modes, and a gradient of obligation
Auto Lambda applies the patch. You roll back if it breaks you.
Function update Lambda applies it WHEN YOU DEPLOY.
Manual You do. Documented for temporary rollback only.
Container images: AWS publishes base images; rebuilding and redeploying is entirely yours.
The middle mode, on a function nobody deploys
“If you don’t update your function, then Lambda doesn’t update the runtime.”
The webhook handler that works. The nightly report. The glue function between two services. Nobody
deploys them because nothing needs changing — so nothing patches them either.
No deadline, and the failure is a cliff
“Lambda doesn’t impose a time limit on how long you can use any particular runtime version.”
“… might eventually experience degraded performance or issues, such as a certificate expiry, which can
cause them to stop working properly.”
PUBLISHED VERSIONS, BY MODE
Auto: runtime updated in phase two of a rollout.
Function update: not updated — a static snapshot of
code, configuration AND runtime.
Perfect rollback artefact. Also a frozen runtime.
ENFORCE IT, DO NOT REQUEST IT
deny PutRuntimeManagementConfig
→ “causes all functions to default to the Auto mode”
Organisation-wide by SCP. For customer-managed
runtimes, also deny lambda:AssociateRuntimeVersion.
All the ambiguity is in one word — “regularly” — and that word is yours to define. Manual mode on $LATEST
also blocks CPU architecture changes, so a forgotten rollback becomes a migration you cannot do.
Keep a list of functions whose runtime version is older than their last deployment. Nothing in Lambda builds it for you.
